questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Define a capriccio and state what it assembles
questions.stem: A dispatcher reviewing a wall panel found a picture that sets an Italian campanile beside a northern quay and a bronze horse that was never cast. What is such a picture called and what does it assemble?

options.text: A capriccio, which assembles buildings and objects from different places into one invented scene
A veduta, which records a single city square exactly as the artist saw it
options.misconception: confuses an invented assembly with a topographical record

options.text: A cartoccio, which draws a plan of the yard to scale for the engineers
options.misconception: treats the picture as a technical drawing

options.text: A scherzo, which jests with the traffic in the picture purely for comic effect
options.misconception: reduces the invention to a joke about the scene

questions.explanation: A capriccio combines elements from different places into one scene that never existed as a whole. Calling it a record of a single square or a working plan removes the invention that defines it.
questions.hint: The picture gathers things that were never together.

questions.stem: An artist sketching the roof beams asked why a cartoon is pricked through before it is painted. Write one sentence explaining what the pricking does for the finished picture.

answer.exemplar: The pricking marks the design in a row of tiny holes so that the drawing can be pounced onto the panel and traced in paint, which lets the finished picture sit exactly over its underdrawing instead of drifting as the painter works freehand across the whole surface.

questions.explanation: Pricking transfers the design by pouncing, so the paint sits exactly over the underdrawing. Treating the holes as decoration or as loose guidelines ignores their mechanical purpose.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of foreground strokes in a graded landscape
questions.stem: In the yard landscape the foreground is painted with three times as many brushstrokes as the middle distance, and the middle distance has four times as many as the far distance. If the far distance carries 5 strokes, how many strokes does the foreground carry?

questions.hint: Work outwards from the far distance in two steps.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a nocturne requires in order to be read
questions.stem: A painter's patron asked why a night scene must be painted in a certain way. Write one sentence explaining what a nocturne requires in order to be read.

answer.exemplar: A nocturne must be painted so that its forms resolve only under lamplight, with the lit areas built up in thin, soft gradations and the darks kept open rather than loaded, because the effect depends on the eye's adjustment to a low, artificial light rather than on daylight alone.

questions.explanation: A nocturne depends on how paint behaves under lamplight, so its forms are built for that light. Treating the darkness as simply a black area or as a daylight scene misses the requirement.
questions.hint: Think about the light the picture is read by.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how graded handling produces distance in a landscape

stimulus.body: The note on the landscape above the booking office reads: near leaves are laid in with a loaded brush and a hard edge, the middle distance in shorter strokes of a duller green, and the far hills in a thin grey wash with the panel left showing through. options.misconception: reduces the far band to untouched ground only

options.text: By using one uniform touch throughout, so the eye reads the whole panel as one plane
options.misconception: mistakes a flat uniform handling for graded distance

options.text: By grading the handling from thick and sharp near the eye to thin and pale in the distance

questions.explanation: The note describes a graded handling from a loaded, hard-edged brush to a thin wash, which is what makes the space read as deep. Treating the bands as uniform, crossed or merely unpainted misses that.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a capriccio can evoke a place more strongly than a record
questions.stem: Night work in the marshalling yard turned to a picture of a harbour that never existed. Write one sentence explaining how the capriccio can evoke a place more strongly than a record of it.

answer.exemplar: A capriccio evokes a place more strongly than a record because it assembles the parts that memory keeps and drops the ones that do not, so a tower from one port, a crane from another and a figure from a third combine into a city the viewer recognises as a kind of place rather than as a specific spot.

questions.explanation: A capriccio builds a suggestive whole from remembered parts, which can feel truer to a place than a record. Reading it as a document or a joke removes the imaginative work it does.
questions.hint: Think about what is left out and what is combined.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the unlit width of a panel in a lamplight test
questions.stem: In the dispatcher's test room the reading lamp throws a cone 3.00 m wide at the panel's distance, and the nocturne panel is 1.60 m wide and hung centred. How many centimetres of the panel's width fall outside the lamp's cone?
questions.explanation: The lit cone is 3.00 m wide and the panel only 1.60 m, so 3.00 - 1.60 = 1.40 m, that is 140 cm, of the cone falls outside the panel. Subtracting the other way round gives a negative figure.
questions.hint: Compare the lit width with the panel width.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A pricked cartoon under finished paint
questions.learningObjective: Infer the order of work from pricking holes in a capriccio

stimulus.body: The capriccio of the tower and the quay was painted over an earlier sheet, and the underdrawing shows a grid of pricking holes for the tower's masonry courses. The catalogue notes that the holes run from the base of the tower up to the belfry and stop short of the roof, and that the painted tower does the same.

questions.stem: What do the pricking holes in the tower tell us about the order of work on this capriccio?

options.text: That the panel was reused from a picture of a real stone tower
options.misconception: invents a reuse from a transferred design

options.text: That the tower was painted first and the holes added later by an assistant
options.misconception: reverses the sequence the evidence shows

options.text: That the design was transferred and then painted, so the holes guide forms built afterwards
That the roof was added after the belfry, since the holes stop short
options.misconception: reads an unfinished edge as a later addition

questions.explanation: The holes are a transferred underdrawing that the painted tower follows, so the design came first and the paint after it. Reversing the sequence, inventing a reuse or reading a stopped edge as a later addition contradicts the note.
questions.hint: The painted tower follows the holes exactly.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what graded handling does and how it differs from order of work
questions.stem: The last of the night scenes shows a far shore laid in thinly. First say what graded handling does; then say how it differs from simply finishing the far part last.

options.text: It makes the picture larger, and it differs by stretching the near strokes
options.misconception: confuses handling with scale

options.text: It makes the far part harder to paint, and it differs only in the time the painter needed
options.misconception: reduces the method to speed of execution

options.text: It makes the picture older in appearance, and it differs by adding a varnish
options.misconception: confuses handling with ageing

options.text: It makes the touch match the distance, and it differs by choosing the handling for the space

questions.explanation: Graded handling makes the touch match the distance, which is a choice about the painting rather than about the order of it. Reducing it to speed, ageing or scale removes what the method actually does.
questions.hint: Ask what the touch is chosen to match.
